papers.title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
papers.abstract: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

papers.title: Reference Coordinates, Output Perturbations, and Information Loss in EEG Decoding
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoders can respond to reference changes that preserve all relative-potential information. We use established measurement-operator theory to distinguish coordinate sensitivity, additional output-channel perturbations, and electrode loss. Exact pseudoinverse alignment supplies a consistency control; measurement-operator canonicalization (MOC) denotes a graph-Tikhonov estimator. The broader evaluation covers three public motor-imagery datasets and four decoders. The primary EEGNet comparison on Cho2017 and PhysioNet uses three paired training seeds, three shared noise realizations, and six front ends, with identical CAR training inputs sharing checkpoints. At 10 dB output perturbation, MOC-minus-raw disagreement was -0.144 and -0.107, while balanced-accuracy differences were 0.044 and 0.050, respectively; these four contrasts passed the retained Holm correction. MOC also reduced disagreement relative to pseudoinversion across all three seeds in both cohorts. However, comparison with fixed graph smoothing after pseudoinversion did not establish an additional MOC benefit. Preserving zero reference rows changed raw disagreement by less than 0.001 in magnitude; inverse-method predictions were unchanged. For canonical front ends, cross-reference disagreement was close to the reference obtained from independent noise within the same operator. Controlled weak-mode reconstruction and equal-rank electrode masks exposed separate stability and information-loss effects. The results locate the complete-reference gains within spatial processing under the specified stress model, while requiring decoding accuracy alongside consistency to assess practical utility.

papers.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce OAK-Mind, a zerO-training, multi-Agent, Knowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

papers.title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
papers.abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability. We then demonstrate that random internal perturbations allow individual bonds to estimate their mechanical dominance and locally adjust their stiffnesses to restore learning capacity. However, the forces associated with active learning bias these local measurements and interfere with restoration. Separating learning and repair into wake-like and sleep-like phases removes this interference and improves continual-learning performance. Our results suggest that the need for offline restorative phases can emerge from the mechanics of physical learning, even in systems without biological components.
